source_read: PMC full text PMC7243091 (JAMA Netw Open 2020;3(5):e204693), read in the app's browser in my own tab; whole article read (Key Points, abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Strengths and Limitations, Conclusions) and the Table read row by row. The four figures are forest plots and the PRISMA flowchart, whose pooled values are given in the text and figure legends; the supplement (eTables 1-6, eMethods 1-10, eFigures 1-5) is a separate PDF and was not opened, so the raw per-study data, the funnel plots, the subgroup heterogeneity statistics and the risk-of-bias scoring could not be checked. The PMC page carries no correction or retraction notice. Text saved to scratchpad/ket-a/s229/beck_2020_full.txt.

claims.overstatement: As far as this source is concerned, two parts of the claim are not supported by it and one needs narrowing, though none is contradicted. (1) 'the changes pass within minutes to a couple of hours of the end of the infusion': Beck et al. describe the symptoms as transient throughout but give no recovery time and state in the Strengths and Limitations that further work is needed to characterise the time course of ketamine's psychotomimetic effects. The claim attributes its timing to Krystal et al. (1994) and Malhotra et al. (1996), which is the right attribution; nothing in the pooled result should be read as supporting it, and the sentence that opens the claim ('the changes pass within minutes to a couple of hours') sits before the Beck sentence, so a reader could take the meta-analysis to be the source. (2) 'with salt water given to the same people on another day as the comparison': in Beck's set the placebo was saline in 35 of the 36 healthy-volunteer studies (one, van Berckel et al. 1998, is 'not reported'), but the conditions were not always on another day. Two of the studies gave ketamine and placebo on the same day, and that design produced a significantly larger total-symptom effect (2.29, 95% CI 1.69-2.89, against 1.39, 1.12-1.66; P = .007), which Beck et al. suggest may reflect unblinding, since one of the two was unblinded and the other single-blind. (3) 'the psychosis-like effect being the larger of the two' is right as a pooled comparison, but Beck et al. note that the two analyses did not rest on the same studies (the negative analysis had an extra continuous-infusion study, the positive analysis more unblinded studies and fewer same-day studies), and they still call the negative effect large. Within those limits the wording does not overstate: the claim keeps the result as an association in screened healthy volunteers during one session, says the figures are peak values, reports the heterogeneity and the small-study asymmetry, and does not repeat the review's recommendation about how ketamine should be given, which would have read as advice.
claims.note: Every Beck number in the statement and magnitude checks out against the Results, and I re-derived the three sample sizes from the Table: the 25 total-symptom studies sum to exactly 491 participants, the 21 positive-symptom studies to 513 and the 22 negative-symptom studies to 527, and all 36 rows sum to 725. Total SMD 1.50 (1.23-1.77), positive 1.55 (1.29-1.81), negative 1.16 (0.96-1.35), all P < .001; positive minus negative 0.36 (0.12-0.61), z = 2.90, P = .004; I2 75.7% (Q 96.57), 74.9% (Q 81.40), 64.6% (Q 66.55); Egger z 4.27, 5.06, 5.12, all P < .001; trim-and-fill 1.37 (1.07-1.67), 1.49 (1.18-1.80), 1.09 (0.89-1.30). The claim's rounded ranges are right: I2 65% to 76% covers 64.6 to 75.7, and Egger z 4.27 to 5.12 covers all three. Note that the abstract instead prints 'I2 range, 77%-83%', which matches none of the three figures in the Results; the claim follows the Results, which is the right choice, and the mismatch should be recorded as a reporting issue. 'Peak values, taken at each study's largest amount and at the rating time with the highest score, so they are the largest effects the studies saw' is supported almost word for word by the Methods ('The highest available ketamine dose was selected if multiple doses were reported') and the Strengths and Limitations, where the authors say they aimed at ketamine's maximal ability to induce symptoms, selected the time point with the highest ketamine-induced score with the matching placebo point, used the highest dose, and conclude that their effect sizes are likely the largest seen with ketamine. 'Within-person placebo-controlled' is an inclusion criterion; the standardisation is by the SD of the within-person difference, with the between-condition correlation assumed to be r = 0.5 for every study (sensitivity analyses at 0.1 and 0.7 are in the supplement, which I could not open). 'Clinician-rated' is accurate for the BPRS and PANSS, though Beck et al. call them standardised assessments rather than clinician-rated. On the claim's wider sentence about blinding, Beck adds support and a qualification: 9 of the 36 healthy-volunteer studies were not double-blind, the authors say blinding participants may be very difficult because the dissociative effects are obvious to participant and personnel, and they suggest a low ketamine dose or midazolam as an active comparator; but blinding status did not change the pooled effect size in any domain, which is a point against functional unblinding driving the result and which the claim does not mention. The claim's figure of 725 is the number of unique healthy volunteers; the three schizophrenia studies in the Table are separate and were not pooled, which the claim does not misstate (it does not cite Beck for the patient data). Nothing in the claim reads as advice on amounts, routes, timing or combinations; the doses it gives are study conditions, and it leaves out the review's own bolus recommendation.

anchors.locator: Results > Retrieved Studies for the Meta-analysis of Healthy Volunteers, 1st paragraph; Table (Summary of Sample and Study Characteristics), all 36 healthy-volunteer rows
anchors.extracted: 36 studies, 725 unique healthy participants (mean [SD] age 28.3 [3.6] years; stated as 533 male [73.6%] and 192 female [26.5%]); ketamine given intravenously in all of them. I summed the Table's sample-size column across the 36 healthy-volunteer rows and get exactly 725. The Table's placebo column reads Saline for 35 rows and 'NR' for one (van Berckel et al., 1998). Blinding: 22 of the rows are double-blind in the BPRS group and 14 in the PANSS group, of which 9 in total are not double-blind (3 'No', 5 'Single', 1 'NR'). The 'Length of ketamine infusion before symptom assessment' column runs from 1 to 120 minutes and is 'NR' for 20 of the 36.

anchors.locator: Results > Total Psychopathological Symptoms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the figure legend between them is not counted as a paragraph); Figure 2
anchors.extracted: Total symptoms: 25 studies, 491 healthy participants (the Table's sample sizes for the 25 cited studies sum to exactly 491); SMD 1.50 (95% CI 1.23-1.77), P < .001; stable in leave-one-out (1.44-1.55); I2 75.7%, Cochran Q 96.57, P < .001; Egger z 4.27, P < .001; trim-and-fill added 3 putative missing studies on the left, giving 1.37 (1.07-1.67); neither age (n = 24 studies) nor sex (n = 22) moderated the effect.

anchors.locator: Results > Positive Psychotic Symptoms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 3
anchors.extracted: Positive symptoms: 21 studies, 513 healthy participants (recomputed from the Table: exactly 513); SMD 1.55 (1.29-1.81), P < .001; leave-one-out 1.47-1.60; I2 74.9%, Q 81.40; Egger z 5.06, P < .001; trim-and-fill 1 putative missing study, giving 1.49 (1.18-1.80); age (n = 20) and sex (n = 19) not moderators.

anchors.locator: Results > Negative Symptoms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 4
anchors.extracted: Negative symptoms: 22 studies, 527 healthy participants (recomputed from the Table: exactly 527); SMD 1.16 (0.96-1.35), P < .001; leave-one-out 1.11-1.19; I2 64.6%, Q 66.55; Egger z 5.12, P < .001; trim-and-fill 2 putative missing studies, giving 1.09 (0.89-1.30); age (n = 20) and sex (n = 19) not moderators.

anchors.locator: Results > Comparison of Positive and Negative Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The ketamine condition was associated more with positive than with negative symptoms: estimate 0.36 (95% CI 0.12-0.61), z = 2.90, P = .004, from a multivariate model with the within-study positive-negative correlation assumed to be 0.5.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Strengths and Limitations, 4th paragraph; Methods > Recorded Variables, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The pooled figures are peak values by design: the authors aimed to determine ketamine's maximal ability to induce psychotomimetic symptoms, took the time point with the highest ketamine-induced symptom score (with the placebo score at the matching point) where several time points were reported, and took the highest dose where several were used, concluding that these effect sizes are likely the largest seen with ketamine. The Methods state the same rule for dose. The same paragraph adds that further work is needed to characterise the dose-response relationship and the time course of the effects, so the review itself establishes no recovery time.

anchors.locator: Results > Total Psychopathological Symptoms > Single-Day vs Multiple-Day Studies; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Against 'salt water given to the same people on another day': 2 of the included studies gave ketamine and placebo on the same day (SMD 2.29, 1.69-2.89) and 17 on different days (1.39, 1.12-1.66), and the same-day design gave a significantly larger total-symptom effect (P = .007). The authors suggest this may reflect unblinding, as one of the two same-day studies was unblinded and the other single-blind with randomised order, or better control of day-to-day variation. For positive and negative symptoms the two designs did not differ.

anchors.locator: Results > Positive Psychotic Symptoms > Infusion Method; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: A source of the heterogeneity the claim reports: studies giving a bolus before the infusion found about twice the positive-symptom effect of studies using a continuous infusion alone (1.63, 1.36-1.90, from 19 studies against 0.84, 0.35-1.33, from 2 studies; P = .006), which the authors attribute to a faster or higher peak concentration. Total and negative symptoms did not differ by infusion method. (Recorded as a study-design factor, not as guidance.)

anchors.locator: Discussion > Strengths and Limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: The review's own limits on the pooled figures: significant inconsistency between studies that the subgroup analyses explain only partly (heterogeneity stayed moderate to high within most subgroups); dose and fasting status too poorly reported to test; four different BPRS versions (16, 20, 18 and 24 items) pooled with few studies stating which items they used; most included studies did not exclude concurrent psychotropic drug use and only a few excluded people with prior ketamine exposure; blinding status did not change the effect size in any domain, although the authors say blinding is very difficult because the dissociative effects are obvious to participants and staff, and they suggest a low dose or midazolam as an active comparator in future.

anchors.locator: Methods > Selection Criteria for the Meta-analysis of Ketamine's Effects in Healthy Volunteers, 1st paragraph; Methods > Statistical Analysis, 2nd to 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Design and comparator as the claim states them: included studies had to be in healthy participants, give subanaesthetic intravenous ketamine (racemic, S- or R-), contain a placebo condition in a within-participant crossover design, and report total, positive or negative BPRS or PANSS scores. The effect size is a standardised mean change, standardised by the SD of the within-person difference between the ketamine and saline conditions, with the between-condition correlation set to r = 0.5 for every study (sensitivity analyses at r = 0.1 and 0.7 in the supplement). I2 bands used: <25% low, 25-75% medium, >75% high.

anchors.locator: Results > Effects of Ketamine in Patients With Schizophrenia, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The schizophrenia part of the review was not pooled: after excluding 7 studies with overlapping data sets, 3 remained and no meta-analysis was possible. Two reported a significant rise in total BPRS, two a significant transient rise in positive symptoms, and of the two that assessed negative symptoms one found a rise and one did not. The authors state that firm conclusions about effects in schizophrenia cannot be drawn. This bears on the claim's framing: the claim cites Beck only for the healthy-volunteer figures, which is right.

anchors.locator: Abstract > Results, read against Results > Total Psychopathological Symptoms, Positive Psychotic Symptoms and Negative Symptoms
anchors.extracted: Internal inconsistency relevant to the claim's heterogeneity figures: the abstract states 'significant inconsistency in outcomes between studies (I2 range, 77%-83%)', while the Results give I2 of 75.7%, 74.9% and 64.6% for the three main analyses. No figure of 77% or 83% appears anywhere in the main text. Two of the three main values fall in the review's own 'medium' band (25-75%), not the 'high' band the abstract's range implies.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Implications for Therapeutic Use of Ketamine, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: On the relevance of the laboratory condition to treatment: the authors note the dose and route used to treat depression (about 0.5 mg/kg intravenously) is similar to those in the pooled studies; that ketamine can induce perceptual disturbances and psychotic symptoms in patients with depression (mean BPRS 12.6, with slightly higher positive scores than the average mean of 7.5 across the BPRS studies pooled here); and that people with a history of psychosis may be more vulnerable. This supports the claim's closing restriction to one session in screened volunteers rather than repeated or non-medical use.

anchors.locator: Methods > Risk of Bias, 1st paragraph; Results > Risk of Bias Across Studies, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Risk of bias was rated with the Newcastle-Ottawa tool for non-randomised studies and the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, with a score of 7 or more counted as low risk; 8 of the included studies were rated high risk, mainly for not documenting parts of the protocol, and the Cochrane assessment across studies gave unclear risk for selection bias and low risk for performance, detection, attrition and reporting bias. Relevant to the claim's low confidence rating and to its blinding sentence: the Newcastle-Ottawa tool is built for cohort and case-control studies, yet 28 of the 36 included studies are described in the Table as randomised within-person crossover studies, and the 'low risk' judgment for performance and detection bias sits awkwardly beside the authors' own statement that blinding is very difficult with ketamine. The scoring itself is in the supplement, which I did not open.

key_findings.correction: I opened the Figure 1 page to check the flowchart and every number matches: 8464 screened in Embase, MEDLINE and PsycINFO; 5896 excluded after title and abstract; 2442 duplicates removed; 126 identified for full-text review or full text sought from authors; 90 full texts or abstracts excluded (28 duplicate data, 25 unable to provide raw data, 22 no placebo condition, 9 independent group design, 3 no intravenous administration or fewer than 2 participants, 2 incorrect symptom items (BPRS), 1 additional compound given); 36 included in the meta-analysis (25 total, 22 negative, 21 positive) and 3 in the systematic review of patients with schizophrenia. 8464 - 5896 - 2442 = 126 and 126 - 90 = 36 both check. The 22 BPRS and 14 PANSS split is right: I counted the Table's two blocks.

Text values confirmed, and I read Figure 2 to check the rest: the forest plot prints Q = 96.57, P < .001, df = 24, I2 = 75.7%, the random-effects estimate 1.50 (1.23-1.77), and 25 study rows whose smallest is Rowland et al. 2005 at 0.49 (-0.17 to 1.15) and largest Nagels et al. 2011 at 3.51 (2.15 to 4.86), exactly as the card gives them. I also summed the Table's sample sizes for the 25 cited studies and get exactly 491.

Figure 3 prints Q = 81.40, df = 20, I2 = 74.9% and 1.55 (1.29-1.81); the 21 rows run from Micallef et al. 2002 at 0.50 (-0.24 to 1.23) to Krystal et al. 1999 at 4.66 (3.15 to 6.17), as the card gives them. The 21 studies' sample sizes sum to exactly 513.

Figure 4 prints Q = 66.55, df = 21, I2 = 64.6% and 1.16 (0.96-1.35); the 22 rows run from Abdallah et al. 2018 at 0.45 (-0.10 to 1.00) to Nagels et al. 2011 at 2.30 (1.33 to 3.26), as the card gives them. The 22 studies' sample sizes sum to exactly 527.

0.36 (0.12-0.61), z = 2.90, P = .004, the assumed within-study correlation of 0.5 with sensitivity analyses at 0.1 and 0.7, and no significant BPRS-versus-PANSS difference in any domain are all at the stated places. (The equation in Methods > Statistical Analysis is an image between two text paragraphs, so the paragraph count there depends on whether the 'where MKet and MSal...' sentence is read as its own paragraph; the card's 4th is defensible.)

The formula, the r = 0.5 assumption and the peak-value rule (highest dose, and the time point with the highest ketamine-induced score with the matching placebo point) are as stated, and the authors do conclude their effect sizes are likely the largest seen with ketamine. The note that a within-person standardised change is not comparable with a between-group SMD and depends on the assumed correlation is sound and important for the claim. The Strengths and Limitations paragraph is the 4th of that subsection, as the card says.

All six subgroup estimates match. I checked the note against Figure 3: the two infusion-only positive-symptom studies are Krystal et al. 2003 at 1.02 (0.55 to 1.50) and Micallef et al. 2002 at 0.50 (-0.24 to 1.23), exactly as the note gives them, and pooling those two reproduces the printed subgroup estimate (I get 0.84, 0.35 to 1.32, against the printed 0.84, 0.35 to 1.33).

Values match, and the two single-day studies are correctly identified as Thiebes et al. 2017 (ref 29) and Kraguljac et al. 2017 (ref 30). The authors do offer unblinding or better control of day-to-day variation as explanations.
All twelve subgroup estimates match the three Blinding Method and Ketamine Preparation subsections.

Matches, with one wording point: the paper says the meta-regressions were against 'sex' and never states the coding, so 'percentage of men' is the card's reading; and four studies with 107 participants give no sex data, which is why the sex meta-regressions rest on 22, 19 and 19 studies as the card's analysis field records. The 'range of mean ages, 22-40 years' is the authors' rounding of the Table's 21.7 to 39.6.

The three studies, their sample sizes (13, 17, 18) and the mapping of findings to papers are right, including that the study finding no negative-symptom increase is Lahti et al. 2001 (ref 26) and the one finding an increase is Malhotra et al. 1998 (ref 27).

18.40 PANSS points and the Clinical Global Impression equivalence are at the stated place, and reference 71 is indeed Leucht et al. (2005), 'What does the PANSS mean?'. The note is right that the review does not say how many studies the 18.40 average covers or whether it is weighted.

I recounted every tally in the Table and get the same: 27 double-blind, 5 single-blind, 3 unblinded, 1 not reported; order randomised in 30 and not in 6; saline placebo in 35 with 1 not reported; the infusion-length-before-rating column is filled for 17 studies (1 to 120 minutes) and 'NR' for 19; 5 studies excluded prior ketamine exposure and most did not exclude concurrent psychotropic drug use.
Instrument, cut-off, the 8 high-risk studies and the across-study Cochrane judgments are as stated.

The heterogeneity account matches the Discussion and Strengths and Limitations. I independently reconstructed the editors' calculation from the study-level estimates and confidence intervals printed in Figures 2 to 4 (SE from the interval width, REML tau-squared, 95% prediction interval with t on k - 2 degrees of freedom) and get the same figures to two decimals: tau 0.57, 0.51 and 0.36, and prediction intervals 0.28 to 2.72 (total), 0.44 to 2.65 (positive) and 0.39 to 1.93 (negative). The reconstruction also reproduces the published pooled estimates and intervals (1.50, 1.23-1.77; 1.55, 1.28-1.81 against the printed 1.29-1.81; 1.16, 0.96-1.35), so the method is sound. The intervals should keep their 'editors' calculation' label, since the review reports no tau-squared.
The 0.5 mg/kg comparison, the 12.6 against 7.5 BPRS comparison, the bolus recommendation and the absence of any pooled patient data are as stated.

reporting_issues.note: I checked all 36 rows and find the same three and only those three: Krystal et al. 1998 (23 participants, 19:11), Morgan et al. 2011 (16, 10:8) and Powers et al. 2015 (19, 10:10). Together they overshoot by 10, which is why the Table's sex columns and sample sizes cannot both be right.

Reproduced exactly: the Table's male column sums to 436 and the female column to 192; four studies (Abdallah 14, Hoflich 30, Krystal 2006 31, D'Souza 2012 32 = 107 participants) report sex as 'NR'; and 725 - 192 = 533, the figure printed. 533/725 is 73.52%, so 73.6% is wrong in the last digit (and 73.6 + 26.5 = 100.1). On age I get the same as the card: unweighted mean of study means 28.14, weighted 27.62, against the printed 28.3. Worth adding that the printed SD of 3.6 is close to the SD of the 34 study means (3.55), which suggests the figure is a mean of study means rather than the participant-level mean its 'mean [SD] age' label implies.

The Discussion calls reference 29 unblinded and reference 30 single-blind with randomised order; the Table has Thiebes et al. (ref 29) as single-blind and randomised and Kraguljac et al. (ref 30) as unblinded and not randomised. The labels are swapped, and the card's conclusion that the explanation still holds for both is right, since neither was double-blind.

Confirmed: performance and detection bias rated low across studies while 9 of the 36 included studies were not double-blind and the authors themselves say blinding is very difficult with ketamine. Also relevant: the Newcastle-Ottawa tool is built for cohort and case-control studies and was applied here to within-person crossover experiments, 30 of which the Table records as randomised.

The criterion reads 'more than 3 positive symptom items' and then lists four, while Kraguljac et al. 2017 is marked 'positive (2)' in the Table, which the footnote defines as three items, and that study is in the positive-symptom list and in Figure 3. The card's reading (the criterion was probably at least 3) is the only one consistent with the analysis as run.

All four checked. The bolus list prints reference 64, which the reference list gives as Lahti et al. (1995), one of the 7 schizophrenia studies excluded for overlapping data, and omits reference 3 (Krystal et al., 2005), which does appear in Figure 3. The total-symptom age meta-regression list begins with reference 5, which the reference list gives as Krystal et al. (1994), not an included study. Figure 2 prints 'D'Souza et al,32 2012' although 32 is Krystal et al. (2006), which appears in the same column with its own row. The psychotropic-exclusion list ends with references 80 and 81 (Musso et al., 2011; Umbricht et al.), which are outside the included range.
References 62 and 63 are Morrison et al. and van de Loo et al., both intranasal esketamine studies, not inhaled.

Reproduced from the reference lists: the total-symptom analysis names 25 studies, the single-day subgroup 2 and the multiple-day subgroup 17, leaving exactly the six the card names (Krystal et al. 2006, Grent-'t-Jong et al. 2018, Hoflich et al. 2015, Abdallah et al. 2018, Morgan et al. 2011, Nagels et al. 2011) unassigned, with no explanation.

The Figure 1 box reads '36 Included in the meta-analysis' with 25, 22 and 21 beneath it and '3 Included in the systematic review of patients with schizophrenia', while only one of those three (Malhotra et al., 1997) is also a healthy-volunteer study, so 38 distinct reports are used.
The sentence gives neither the scale (total or positive BPRS) nor a citation attached to the 12.6, and the 7.5 average is not defined either (which studies, weighted or not).

'P < .008' is printed as the card says. I also reproduced the subgroup estimate from the two Figure 3 studies and get 0.84 (0.35 to 1.32) against the printed 0.84 (0.35 to 1.33), so the editors' check holds.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 is the right instrument for a systematic review with meta-analysis (METHODS 5.3), the vocabulary is AMSTAR 2's, 'no-information' for item 7 with a provisional overall rating is the documented extension, and low confidence follows from one unmet critical item (no protocol or registration, which I confirmed: the review names MOOSE and PRISMA only and no registration appears anywhere in the text). I reach the same judgments on the items I can check from the main text: PICO specified; designs not explained; a three-database search with dates and keywords but no registries, grey literature or reference-list searching; selection and extraction in duplicate; the Table describing studies but not doses; Newcastle-Ottawa applied to crossover experiments with a summary cut-off; no funding of included studies; appropriate random-effects methods with sensitivity and leave-one-out analyses; a blinding subgroup analysis but no separate analysis of the 8 high-risk studies; risk of bias discussed but not carried into the abstract; heterogeneity examined; publication bias examined in Results only. Two points I could not verify: item 7 depends on Supplement eMethods 1, which I did not open either, so the provisional label is right; and item 16 (conflicts and funding) sits in the collapsed 'Article notes' panel, which I could not read in the PMC view, so I can neither confirm nor dispute the 'yes'. The reasoning's closing limits on how the review may be cited match what I found, in particular that it supports nothing about the duration of the symptoms.

interpretation_gap.note: Agree with 'substantial', and every element of the card's 'claimed' paragraph checks out against the text: the abstract and conclusions turn a between-study contrast of 19 studies against 2 into a recommendation about how ketamine should be given; the abstract states the subgroup findings causally ('increased'); the Key Points say the increase was found 'in healthy volunteers and patients with schizophrenia' although no meta-analysis was possible in schizophrenia and one of the two studies rating negative symptoms found no increase; the significant Egger tests appear only in Results; and the symptoms are called transient throughout although no rating after the session was analysed and the authors say the time course still needs characterising. I would add one more item to this paragraph: the abstract's heterogeneity figure ('I2 range, 77%-83%') matches none of the three values in Results (75.7%, 74.9%, 64.6%), two of which fall in the review's own 'medium' band, so the abstract overstates the inconsistency it reports while understating nothing else.

missed: The abstract reports 'significant inconsistency in outcomes between studies (I2 range, 77%-83%)', which matches none of the three I2 values in the Results (75.7%, 74.9% and 64.6%) and no subgroup value given in the main text. This belongs with the reporting issues: it is the figure a reader of the abstract alone would carry away, and the claim's heterogeneity range is taken, rightly, from the Results instead.

Overlap between this meta-analysis and the single studies cited beside it (METHODS 6.3, overlapping evidence): Newcomer et al. (1999) is one of Beck's pooled studies (reference 31, in both the total and the positive analyses), so a claim that cites Beck and then Newcomer as separate support is counting one study twice. Malhotra et al. (1997), the schizophrenia companion of Malhotra et al. (1996), is likewise pooled (reference 25). Krystal et al. (1994) is not among the 36 (it appears only as the stray reference 5 in a meta-regression list), so that one is independent.

Author overlap in the other direction: three of the twelve review authors (Driesen, D'Souza and Krystal) are authors of eight of the included studies (Driesen et al. 2013; D'Souza et al. 2012 and 2018; Krystal et al. 1998, 1999, 2003, 2005 and 2006). The card notes under AMSTAR item 16 that the review does not discuss this; it is worth stating on the card itself, because those eight studies carry a large share of the pooled samples.

The Table's 'Length of ketamine infusion before symptom assessment' column shows that, in the 17 studies that report it, the rating was taken between 1 and 120 minutes after the infusion began, that is during or at the end of the session. Together with the peak-value rule this fixes what the pooled figures describe: symptoms at their height during the session, with nothing measured afterwards. The card's interpretation_gap makes the second half of this point; the timing column is the direct evidence for it.
